lines: The last topic opened the cache that sits in front of a slow disk.
But a change that only ever lived in that cache disappears completely the instant the process stops running before it's written back.
So something has to exist that survives a crash even when the cache itself doesn't.
That something turns out to have its own position, read directly off a live cluster rather than assumed.
Checked before and after a real write, that position only ever moves forward, never back.
And the real distance between those two readings turns out to be an exact count, not a rough guess.
Worth checking whether every single change really pays for its own separate trip to make that log durable.
A real batch of changes happening close together in time, measured directly, shares a single one of those trips across many of them at once.
Nothing about sharing that trip lets any individual change skip waiting for it to finish first.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A disk doesn't write an entire page in one physical step. It writes several smaller physical pieces, one after another.
If power fails partway through, does the result always come out as either every piece landing or none of them?
answer: It doesn't, and that gap is exactly why a separate defense has to exist at all.
Some of those smaller pieces can land on disk while others never do, leaving a result that's part old and part new.
Nothing reading that result afterward can tell which parts actually finished.

lines: Here's that defense shown directly, not just argued for.
A real page, changed twice right after a real save point. Measured directly, the full defense against exactly that mixed-up result fires once, on the first change.
The second change to that same page doesn't trigger it again, because nothing about the risk changed.
A completely different piece of this same machinery is worth checking the same way.
Several genuinely different system-level ways exist to force a write all the way out to physical storage rather than leave it sitting in some cache along the way.
Read directly off this sandbox's own cluster, one specific one of those ways turns out to actually be in use, not an abstraction standing in for all of them.
A different engine runs into the identical mixed-up-page risk.

Named here directly from its own documentation rather than run in this sandbox, that engine reaches for a genuinely different fix: a safety copy, written somewhere else first, checked during recovery instead of trusting the original location at all.
One real, documented failure is worth naming directly rather than glossed over.
A system once discovered that a failed attempt to force data all the way out to disk could come back claiming success anyway, even though the write never actually landed.
Once that's even possible, the only response anyone can still trust is starting over completely: stop, and rebuild everything from the last point known to be good.
Pulling the whole topic back together.
That position in the log, moving only forward by an exact measured amount. A real batch of changes sharing far fewer separate durability trips than it has changes.
A real mixed-up-page defense that fires exactly once per save point, not on every single change. One specific, chosen way to force a write all the way out, confirmed directly.
A different engine's own different answer to the identical risk. And the hard lesson that a failed attempt to force data out can never be safely assumed to just need retrying.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.

A monitoring script sees one of those force-out attempts fail, just once. It writes a warning and lets everything keep running rather than stopping it, reasoning that a single failure probably doesn't matter much.
Is that response actually safe, and why or why not?
answer: It isn't safe, for exactly the reason this topic already named directly.

The whole point of that hard lesson is that once a failed force-out attempt can happen without the caller reliably finding out, nothing the caller believes about what already landed on disk can be trusted anymore.
Writing a warning and continuing keeps running on exactly that untrustworthy belief. Stopping and rebuilding from the last known-good point is the only response that doesn't.
